title: The Kingdom That Ended at His Birth: Strabo, the Nile, and the Seventeen Books
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cnossus, Dorylaus is sent for mercenaries
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. Strabo dates the episode only by the reign of Mithridates V Euergetes (c.150-120 BC) at Geography 10.4.10; the year here is an ordering device. Note a contradiction inside Strabo himself: 12.3.33 calls Dorylaus the tactician 'my mother's grandfather', while 10.4.10 makes Lagetas the brother of Strabo's maternal grandmother, which would put the tactician a generation further back. Not resolved here.
stops.campa: Mithridates Euergetes wants soldiers and sends his friend Dorylaus, an expert in the arranging of armies, to hire them where they are best. Dorylaus crosses to Crete and is still there when word comes that the king has been murdered at Sinope. The Cnossians, at war with Gortyn, elect the stranded Pontic officer their general; he wins their war, marries a Macedonian woman named Sterope, and fathers Lagetas and Stratarchas on the island. A lifetime later a descendant sets the episode down in a book about the shape of the world, and adds that he saw Stratarchas himself, an extremely old man.
suggested_refs: The palace site and Roman-era city of Cnossus, where the Pontic branch of the family was founded
sources: Strabo, Geography 10.4.10 (Loeb, H.L. Jones, via LacusCurtius/Penelope)

stops.name: Comana Pontica, the priesthood of the second Dorylaus
stops.date_confidence: the fact is attested at Geography 12.3.33; Strabo gives no year, and the date is an ordering device inside the reign of Mithridates VI. Coordinates are the sanctuary hill south of Gumenek on the west bank of the Yesilirmak, nine kilometres northeast of Tokat.
stops.campa: A second Dorylaus, son of Philetaerus and nephew of the tactician, is raised as the foster-brother of Mithridates Eupator and comes into everything a king can give: honours, office, and the priesthood of Comana. The sanctuary he receives holds thousands of temple servants, a goddess the Greeks call Ma, and a countryside that empties into the precinct for the festivals. Twice a year the image of the goddess is carried out in procession, and the priest walks behind it wearing a diadem, second in the kingdom to the king himself.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Ma at Comana Pontica and its biennial exodus of the goddess, Geography 12.3.32-36

stops.name: Comana Pontica, the kingdom offered to Rome
stops.date_confidence: attested as an event at Geography 12.3.33, undated by Strabo; the year orders the segment. Strabo tells the same fall twice and does not name the same man both times: at 12.3.33 it is Dorylaus son of Philetaerus who is caught, at 10.4.10 the Loeb renders it of Lagetas. The contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: The priest of Comana is caught trying to make the kingdom revolt to the Romans. He is overthrown, and the whole house is cast into disrepute along with him: the priesthood gone, the royal intimacy withdrawn, a generation of Pontic notables suddenly on the wrong side of a king who does not forgive. Whichever kinsman it was who reached for Rome, and the two passages do not agree, the punishment fell on all of them together. Strabo sets the ruin down in one clause and moves on.
suggested_refs: Inger N.I. Kuin, 'Rewriting Family History: Strabo and the Mithridatic Wars' (2017)

stops.name: Phasis, Moaphernes set over Colchis
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 11.2.18 and 12.3.33 that Moaphernes came into distinction just before the kingdom's dissolution and was tied to Colchis; no year is given and no evidence places Strabo himself here. Coordinates are the mouth of the Phasis near modern Poti.
stops.campa: Long after the disgrace, Moaphernes, the uncle of Strabo's mother, comes back into favour and is set over Colchis, the far corner of the kingdom where the Phasis comes down out of the Caucasus into the Black Sea. It is a country of linen and hemp and wax and pitch, and of a river Greek ships have been rowing up since the Argo. He holds it in the last good years, when Mithridates still commands from the Bosporus to the Caucasus and the legions are already in Anatolia.
suggested_refs: Strabo's account of Colchis and the Phasis, Geography 11.2.15-19

stops.name: Cabeira, the killing of Tibius and Theophilus
stops.date_confidence: the killings are attested at Geography 12.3.33 and tied to the war with Lucullus; Strabo names no place and no year. Cabeira is chosen because it was Mithridates's seat during the Lucullan campaign of the early 70s BC and is described at 12.3.30. The location is inference, not testimony.
stops.campa: Lucullus is in Pontus and the king is losing. In the royal camp Mithridates puts to death Tibius, cousin of Strabo's maternal grandfather, and Tibius's son Theophilus. The house had already been cast into disrepute once, in the priest's time. Strabo gives the killing in a single clause, without a scene and without a reason, and then gives the consequence: his grandfather, alienated by wrath at the two deaths and seeing that the king's cause is going badly, sets out to avenge both them and himself.
suggested_refs: Lucullus's Pontic campaign and the siege operations around Cabeira, 72-71 BC

stops.name: Amaseia, fifteen garrisons go over to Lucullus
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 12.3.33; Strabo names neither the garrisons nor a date. Placed at his own city, in the middle of the fortress country of the Iris, as the region the defection covered. Month and day default.
stops.campa: He takes pledges from Lucullus and delivers fifteen garrisons. The strongholds of the Iris and the Lycus, fortified rocks with cisterns cut into them and treasure inside, go over to Rome at the word of one Pontic nobleman with a grievance, and Lucullus makes him great promises in return. Three generations of the family had served the house he is handing over. The grandson sets the whole of it down in his geography, and nothing in the passage says what he made of it.
suggested_refs: Kuin, 'Rewriting Family History' (2017), on the arc as active reshaping of family memory for a Roman world

stops.name: Sinope, Pompey and the promise unpaid
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 12.3.33 that Pompey took as enemies all who had favoured Lucullus and that the Senate refused to ratify the promised honours. The 66 BC date is the year of Pompey's supersession of Lucullus; the Pontic settlement follows over the next years. Sinope is the royal capital, not a stated location for the family.
stops.campa: Pompey arrives to finish the war Lucullus began, and treats every man Lucullus favoured as an inconvenience. The Senate will not ratify the honours promised to the Pontic defectors: it is unjust, runs the argument, that one man should bring a war to a successful issue and another hand out the prizes. Strabo's grandfather receives nothing at all. Sinope, the royal capital, birthplace of Mithridates, passes into the Roman province, and the kingdom is carved into administrative districts under Roman law.
suggested_refs: The Pompeian settlement of Pontus and its eleven city districts, 64-63 BC

stops.name: Amaseia, born in the valley of the Iris
stops.date_confidence: contested on two counts. The birth year 64/63 BC is a modern chronographic reconstruction, not an ancient datum; Roller (2014) argues for no later than c.60 BC, and Pothecary (1999) holds the traditional date less secure than usually assumed. The two are not reconciled. Birthplace is inference too: Strabo calls Amaseia 'my city' (12.3.39) and 'my fatherland' (12.3.15) but nowhere writes that he was born in it. Month and day default.
stops.campa: He is born in a city wedged into a gorge, where the Iris runs deep and fast between rocks so steep the town has to climb them. Above the roofs are the tombs of the Pontic kings cut into the cliff, and higher still the citadel, with water channels driven down through the stone to the river. The kingdom that built all of it has just been taken apart by Rome. He will call the place my city in a book written for readers who have never heard of it, and he never once writes the sentence I was born here.
stops.quote: My city is situated in a large deep valley, through which flows the Iris River. Both by human foresight and by nature it is an admirably devised city... Within this circuit are both the palaces and monuments of the kings.
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 12.3.39, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The rock-cut Pontic royal tombs above Amasya and the citadel water stair
sources: Duane Roller, The Geography of Strabo (Cambridge, 2014), introduction

stops.name: Amaseia, under the tombs of the kings
stops.date_confidence: the description is attested at Geography 12.3.39, written by Strabo as an adult; nothing in the text narrates his childhood. The date is an ordering device only.
stops.campa: The circuit of the walls holds both the palaces and the monuments of the kings, and the boy grows up beneath them: royal graves cut into living rock above the market, standing open; a citadel taken by Roman siege within living memory; two bridges over the river. He will describe the country round it the way a man describes his own fields, by name and by yield, and the ruins in the same tone as the vineyards. Amaseia is now the seat of a Roman assize district.
stops.quote: flowing past the very wall of Amaseia, my fatherland, a very strongly fortified city, flows on into Phanaroea
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 12.3.15, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Roller, A Historical and Topographical Guide to the Geography of Strabo (2018), on Amaseia

stops.name: Cabeira, the strongholds standing empty
stops.date_confidence: the descriptions are attested (Cabeira at Geography 12.3.30; Kainon Chorion, the treasure rock, at 12.3.31, whose location is disputed and is not Niksar). Strabo makes no personal-visit claim distinct from native knowledge, and the date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: At Cabeira there had been a palace, a water-mill, hunting grounds, mines and a park; Mithridates kept a court here, and it was near here that Lucullus broke him. Pompey afterwards made the place a city and called it Diospolis. Strabo inventories the forts of his home province flatly, in the tone of a man listing furniture. Not far off, on a rock sheer on every side with a spring on its summit, stood Kainon Chorion, the New Place, where the king kept his most valuable things until the Romans carried them away.
suggested_refs: The disputed identification of Kainon Chorion among the fortress rocks of the Lycus valley

stops.name: Zela, the Persian gods on the mound
stops.date_confidence: attested as description at Geography 11.8.4 and 12.3.37; Strabo states no personal visit. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Zela stands on a mound the Greeks say Semiramis raised, walled around, and inside it are the Persian gods: Anaitis, Omanus, Anadatus, served with rites the Persians carried west and never let go of. The people of the district come here to swear their most serious oaths. Iranian fire, an Anatolian mother goddess, Greek cities on the coast and a Roman assize court all sit within two days' ride of each other. He will write about other people's gods for sixty years without once calling them strange. The boy is raised inside that arrangement.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary mound at Zile and the Anaitis cult of Pontic Cappadocia

stops.name: Amisus, the scholar the Romans carried off
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 12.3.16 that Tyrannion the grammarian came from Amisus. That Strabo studied under him is the standard modern reconstruction, generally accepted but not a direct statement in the text; Strabo makes no personal-visit claim for Amisus. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Amisus sits on the Black Sea with its old Athenian colony and its royal quarter, and Lucullus took it. Among the people carried west afterwards is Tyrannion, a grammarian, who ends at Rome sorting the library of Aristotle and teaching Greek to Roman aristocrats for money. Strabo names him among the men Amisus produced, and says nothing further about him. The two of them come from one country and one catastrophe. Whether the boy from Amaseia later sat in that displaced Pontic scholar's Roman schoolroom the text does not quite say.
suggested_refs: Tyrannion of Amisus and the transmission of Aristotle's library at Rome

stops.name: Nysa on the Maeander, the school of Aristodemus
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 14.1.48 that Strabo studied under Aristodemus of Nysa; Strabo gives no date, and the placement before his Roman years is inference. Coordinates are the site in Sultanhisar district, Aydin province.
stops.campa: Nysa is built across a ravine so deep that a torrent runs beneath the city and the theatre sits over the covered channel. Here Aristodemus keeps a school, one of a line of Homeric scholars, and here a boy from Pontus is taught to read the Iliad as a description of the world: that Homer knew the Nile flood, the ocean tides, the peoples of the Black Sea, and that where he looks ignorant he is inventing on purpose. The argument turns up again, unchanged, in the first book of the Geography, sixty years on.
suggested_refs: The theatre and gorge-bridge of Nysa on the Maeander

stops.name: Ephesus, the coast the record does not supply
stops.date_confidence: speculative, and marked as such. No first-person statement about Ephesus survives anywhere in the Geography. The stop stands on the shape of the roads, not on testimony, and the date is invented to order the segment. Treat as the weakest point on this itinerary.
stops.campa: To go from Nysa to Rome a man goes down the Maeander valley to the sea, and the sea is reached at Ephesus, where the great temple stands, the harbour silts, and the road out of the interior ends. Strabo gives the city long sections of Book 14: its Amazon foundation, its temple burnt on the night Alexander was born, its rebuilding by the whole of Asia. Getting him from the Maeander to the Tiber requires this coast. He never once writes that he stood there.
suggested_refs: Strabo's account of Ephesus and the Artemision, Geography 14.1.20-26

stops.name: Rome, an acquaintance with Servilius Isauricus
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, downgraded here from the usual textbook claim. Strabo writes at 12.6.2, in the account of Isaura, only that Publius Servilius surnamed Isauricus was a man 'with whom I was acquainted'. He does not say where, does not mention Rome, and does not mention Caesar. Servilius's death in 44 BC gives a terminus ante quem for the acquaintance and nothing more. The Rome location is the standard modern inference and is flagged as inference. The frequently printed citation 5.3.9 or 5.3.7 for this passage is wrong: Book 5 chapter 3 does not mention him.
stops.campa: Publius Servilius Vatia, called Isauricus for the mountain war that made him, took Isaura and levelled it and then lived long enough to become an institution. Writing about Lycaonia decades later, Strabo says of him only that he was a man with whom he was acquainted. That is the whole of it: no place, no year, no circumstance, no anecdote. Servilius dies in 44, which fixes the acquaintance before that year and fixes nothing else about it. Rome is where a young Greek would have met such a man. Rome is a guess.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 12.6.2, on Isaura and Servilius Isauricus
sources: Roller, The Geography of Strabo (2014), introduction

stops.name: Rome, Xenarchus lecturing, and a Stoic pupil
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 14.5.4 for the connection to Xenarchus of Seleucia and his teaching at Rome; the date is an ordering device. Strabo's own Stoic self-identification is attested (1.2.34 and elsewhere). The often-repeated claim that Athenodorus of Tarsus was his teacher is thinner than textbooks make it and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: Xenarchus of Seleucia taught at Alexandria, then at Athens, and finally at Rome, where he held the friendship of Arius and afterwards of Caesar himself and was honoured into a blind old age. Strabo studied under him. He also calls Zeno ours and sets our school against the Peripatetics, so a Peripatetic's pupil writes as a Stoic, and the Byzantines will remember him as Strabo the Stoic philosopher rather than Strabo the geographer. How a man holds both at once is not something the record explains.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 14.5.4 on Xenarchus; Suda-type Byzantine testimonia naming him a Stoic

stops.name: Rome, the Forum, Selurus on the false Aetna
stops.date_confidence: the event is attested at Geography 6.2.6 and Strabo places it 'recently, in my own time' at a gladiatorial combat in the Forum. He gives no year; the c.35 BC date in circulation is a modern conjecture from that phrase and is carried here only to order the segment. The Circus Maximus, sometimes named as the venue, is wrong: Strabo names the Forum.
stops.campa: Selurus, called the son of Aetna, has been overrunning the country around the mountain with a band, and he is sent up to Rome. At a gladiatorial combat in the Forum they build him a tall scaffold made to look like Aetna and stand him on top of it, and the scaffold is rigged to break apart. It gives way. He drops into cages of wild animals set underneath for the purpose. Strabo records this in a chapter about Sicilian volcanic soil, between a note on the vines and a note on the ash.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 6.2.6, on Aetna, its soil, and the execution of Selurus

segments.name: The Aegean, and the Compass of His Travels

stops.name: Gyaros, the fisherman taken aboard
stops.date_confidence: attested and first-person at Geography 10.5.3. The year follows from Strabo's own statement that Caesar was then at Corinth on his way to celebrate the triumph after Actium, which dates it to 29 BC. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Gyaros is a rock with a small fishing village on it, and it cannot pay its tax. When Strabo puts in there the villagers have chosen a fisherman, one of themselves, to go and ask for relief, and Strabo takes the man aboard his own vessel: Caesar is at Corinth, on his way to celebrate the triumph after Actium. On the crossing the fisherman gives him the figure. The island is assessed one hundred and fifty drachmas, and that is more than the place can bear.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 10.5.3, on Gyaros and the embassy to Octavian

stops.name: Corinth, where Caesar then was
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 10.5.3 that Octavian was at Corinth; Strabo makes no claim to have gone ashore himself, and this stop marks the destination of the petition rather than a documented landfall. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: Octavian is at Corinth with the eastern half of the empire settled behind him, moving toward Rome and the triple triumph. Petitions reach him from everywhere, and one of them is being carried by a fisherman from an island of a few hundred people who cannot raise a hundred and fifty drachmas. Strabo names Corinth as the place where Caesar then was and says nothing about going ashore himself. Whether the island got its remission the Geography does not report.
suggested_refs: The refounded Roman colony of Corinth as Octavian's station in 29 BC

stops.name: Populonia, the western limit of the claim
stops.date_confidence: the range claim is attested at Geography 2.5.11, where Strabo says he travelled west as far as the regions of Tyrrhenia opposite Sardinia. He names no town. Populonia is a representative point chosen for that coast, not a place Strabo mentions in connection with himself, and the date is invented to order the segment.
stops.campa: He claims a range: westward as far as the regions of Tyrrhenia opposite Sardinia, eastward as far as Armenia, and from the Black Sea south to the frontiers of Ethiopia. The western end is a stretch of coast rather than a place; he names no town on it. Populonia stands on that headland above the iron of Elba, the one Etruscan city the Etruscans built on the sea itself. Ore comes over from the island to be worked on the mainland, and the furnaces show from the water at night.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 2.5.11, the statement of his own travelled range
sources: Strabo, Geography 5.2.6 (Populonia and the iron of Aethalia)

stops.name: Artaxata, the eastern limit of the claim
stops.date_confidence: the range claim to Armenia is attested at Geography 2.5.11; Strabo names no Armenian city, narrates no itinerary, and gives no date. Artaxata is chosen as the country's capital in this period and is this file's choice, not Strabo's. Date invented to order the segment.
stops.campa: The eastern end of the same claim is Armenia, and Armenia in these decades means Artaxata, set on a peninsula where the Araxes takes in the Metsamor, water on three sides, laid out according to the story by Hannibal for King Artaxias. For his own passage through the country he supplies no road and no season. What he does supply is the country itself, at length: its horse pastures, its royal residences, its long tug between Rome and Parthia, its lake that turns wood to stone.
suggested_refs: The mound of Artaxata beside Khor Virap, at the confluence of the Araks and Metsamor

segments.name: Up the Nile with the Prefect

stops.name: Alexandria, the long residence
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, though a strong one. Extended residence is inferred from the density of firsthand Alexandrian material in Book 17 and is accepted by Roller (2014) and Dueck (2000). Strabo nowhere states how long he stayed. There is no evidence at all that he worked in the Library; that detail is later romance. Coordinates inherited from the canonical Alexandria pin already in use.
stops.campa: He settles in the city where geography was invented. Eratosthenes measured the earth here and laid a grid over it; the Museum has its covered walk, its dining hall, its endowment, its scholars kept at public expense. Book 17 will carry more firsthand detail than any other part of the seventeen: the harbours, the Heptastadion, the run of the streets, the shape of the ground. Whether he ever worked inside the Library is not stated by him or by anyone else, and nothing supplies it.
suggested_refs: The Museion and Brucheion quarter of Alexandria, described at Geography 17.1.8-10
sources: Roller, The Geography of Strabo (2014), introduction

stops.name: Arsinoe on the Red Sea, the fleet he does not sail with
stops.date_confidence: the Arabian expedition is narrated at Geography 16.4.22-24; the staging of the fleet on the Egyptian Red Sea coast is reconstruction. The important point is negative and is attested by silence: Strabo never claims to have gone into Arabia, and his account is built from Gallus and other testimony. The common secondary-literature claim that he was an eyewitness there is wrong.
stops.campa: Aelius Gallus, prefect of Egypt, is assembling a fleet on the Red Sea for the invasion of Arabia Felix. Strabo is in Egypt and knows the prefect well enough to travel with him later. He will write the fullest surviving account of the campaign, the wells and the marches and the disease that killed more Romans than any Arabian did, and the farthest point reached, a city called Marsiaba of the Rhammanitae, subject to Ilasarus, besieged six days and abandoned for want of water. All of it he has from other men. He does not sail.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 16.4.22-24, the Aelius Gallus expedition; the disputed modern identification of Marsiaba with Marib

stops.name: Heliopolis, the houses of the priests
stops.date_confidence: attested and first-person plural at Geography 17.1.29. Month and day are ordering devices within the Egyptian journey of c.25-24 BC.
stops.campa: At Heliopolis the priests' houses are still standing, and the party is walked through them and shown the rooms where Plato and Eudoxus are said to have lodged for thirteen years while the priests taught them the length of the year. Strabo writes the visit in the first person plural, one of the few passages where he stops compiling and is shown around. The city is mostly deserted now: the temple standing in the old manner, the obelisks, the sacred bulls in their enclosures, and the schools he is shown standing empty.
stops.quote: at Heliopolis the houses of the priests and schools of Plato and Eudoxus were pointed out to us
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 17.1.29, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The obelisk of Senusret I at Matariya, last standing element of Heliopolis

stops.name: Giza, the pyramids described but not sworn to
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction. The description at Geography 17.1.33-34 is not marked with an explicit first-person statement of seeing, unlike Heliopolis, Thebes, Syene and Philae, which are. Personal autopsy is plausible and unconfirmed, and the distinction is Strabo's own habit, not a modern nicety. Date is an ordering device.
stops.campa: Beyond Memphis, on the Libyan side of the river, on a rocky brow above the plain, stand the three pyramids, two of them among the seven wonders. Strabo describes the one with a stone in its side that can be taken out, opening on a sloping passage down to a chamber with a coffin in it. He gives the measurements, the quarry the stone came from, the mound of chippings left over from the cutting. What he does not do here, and does elsewhere on this same journey, is say that he saw it.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 17.1.33-34, on the pyramids and the mound of chippings

stops.name: Thebes, the Colossus at the first hour
stops.date_confidence: attested, explicitly first-person, at Geography 17.1.46. Month and day are ordering devices within the Egyptian journey.
stops.campa: The two seated colossi face the river, one of them broken across the middle by an earthquake, and the broken one makes a noise once a day, around the first hour. Strabo is standing there with Aelius Gallus and the crowd of friends and soldiers around him, and he hears it. He is a guest of the prefect, in a party of officers, on the west bank at the first hour of the day. He records the sound. He records that it might come from the stones, or from the people gathered at the base, and then declines to say which.
stops.quote: I too, when I was present at the places with Aelius Gallus and his crowd of associates, both friends and soldiers, heard the noise at about the first hour
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 17.1.46, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The Colossi of Memnon on the Theban west bank, and the Greek and Latin visitor inscriptions on the northern statue

stops.name: Syene, the frontier of Ethiopia
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 2.5.12, where Strabo states the ascent as far as Syene and the frontiers of Ethiopia in his own voice; the surrounding Book 17 material is the fullest firsthand writing in the work. The frequent citation of 17.1.50 for this quoted claim is wrong; 17.1.50 is the wagon passage to Philae. Month and day are ordering devices.
stops.campa: He goes as far up the river as the empire does. At Syene there is a well by which Eratosthenes showed the sun stands vertical at the summer solstice, and on Elephantine a Nilometer, a shaft of cut stone marked off with the rise of the river and watched by priests because the taxes are set from it; the readings go out from there to the rest of the country. Beyond are three Roman cohorts on garrison, the cataract, and the frontier of Ethiopia. He never writes of going further south than this.
stops.quote: ascended the Nile as far as Syene and the frontiers of Ethiopia
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 2.5.12, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The Nilometer on Elephantine Island and the well of Syene used in Eratosthenes's measurement

stops.name: Philae, the wagon across the level plain
stops.date_confidence: attested and first-person plural at Geography 17.1.50. Month and day are ordering devices; this is the southern limit of the personally travelled itinerary.
stops.campa: From Syene to Philae the party goes by wagon across an exceedingly level plain, about a hundred stadia in all, past the cataract where the Nile breaks over black rock and the boatmen run the rapids in front of the Roman officers for money. On the island there is a temple, and a sacred bird the Egyptians call a hawk, which is brought out and shown to them; Strabo looks at it and writes that it seemed to him unlike any hawk he had seen. Then the party turns north.
stops.quote: We went to Philae from Syene by wagon through an exceedingly level plain, a distance all told of about one hundred stadia.
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 17.1.50, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: The island temple of Philae, relocated to Agilkia in the 1970s

segments.name: The Seventeen Books and Their Monsters

stops.name: Amaseia, the forty-seven books that did not survive
stops.date_confidence: the Historika Hypomnemata is attested by Strabo's own cross-references, including 'the sixth book of my Historika Hypomnemata' and 'the second book of my continuation of Polybius' at Geography 11.9.3; the reconstruction at roughly 47 books is Lindsay (2014). Neither the date nor the place of composition is known, and the pin is Strabo's own city, used because Roller argues the final work was completed there. Stated as inference.
stops.campa: Before the geography there are the histories: some forty-seven books, of which he cites his own sixth and calls it the second book of his continuation of Polybius. Polybius stopped at 146. Strabo carries the account forward into his own century, through the Mithridatic wars that ruined his family. Of roughly sixty-four books he is known to have written, seventeen came through. Fragments of the rest survive in other men's quotations, and nothing else does.
suggested_refs: Hugh Lindsay, 'Strabo and the Shape of his Historika Hypomnemata' (2014)

stops.name: Amaseia, Homer arraigned and defended
stops.date_confidence: the passage is attested verbatim at Geography 1.2.35. The composition date and place are unknown; the pin is Strabo's own city and the date orders the segment. This is the passage where dog-headed men actually appear in Strabo, attributed to Aeschylus, and it is often wrongly said not to exist anywhere in the work.
stops.campa: He opens the whole work by arguing that Homer founded geography and that the poets who filled the edges of the world with monsters were not ignorant but deliberate. Hesiod's half-dog men, his long-headed men, his Pygmies; Alcman's web-footed men; Aeschylus's dog-headed men, and men with eyes in their breasts, and one-eyed men. Nobody, Strabo says, charges those poets with not knowing better. They wove myth in on purpose, to gratify the taste for the marvellous, over a real geography they had.
stops.quote: no one could charge Hesiod with ignorance when he speaks of men who are half-dog, of long-headed men and of Pygmies; ... nor Alcman when he tells about web-footed men; nor Aeschylus when he speaks of dog-headed men, or of men with eyes in their breasts, or of one-eyed men
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 1.2.35, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 1.2.35, and its list of named unreliable writers on India: Deimachus, Megasthenes, Onesicritus, Nearchus, with Ctesias among the earlier offenders

stops.name: Amaseia, Pytheas called an arch-falsifier
stops.date_confidence: attested as textual engagement at Geography 1.4.3 and 2.4.1, where Strabo attacks Pytheas of Massalia by name. Place and date of composition unknown; pin is Strabo's own city and the date orders the segment. This is a one-directional relation: Strabo reads and refutes a man four centuries dead.
stops.campa: Pytheas of Massalia sailed north four centuries earlier, reported a place where sea and land and air were none of them separate, and named Thule. Strabo calls him a falsifier, denies he ever made the voyage at all, and throws out his measurements as a matter of principle. Then, refuting him, he copies out enough of Pytheas to preserve him: including the passages where Pytheas marks off carefully what he saw from what he was told, which is the method Strabo works by himself. Most of what survives of Pytheas survives inside that refutation.
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 1.4.3 and 2.4.1, the surviving fragments of Pytheas preserved inside their own refutation

stops.name: Amaseia, Megasthenes beyond all bounds
stops.date_confidence: attested verbatim at Geography 15.1.57-58. Place and date of composition unknown; pin is Strabo's own city, date orders the segment. Note for the record: no dog-headed men appear in Book 15. The nearest thing there is the Monommati, who have dog's ears; the dog-headed men are in Book 1, out of Aeschylus.
stops.campa: Megasthenes went to Chandragupta's court as an ambassador and came back with India. Strabo relays him at length: people with no mouths, living near the sources of the Ganges on the smell of roasted meat and fruit and flowers; people who outrun horses; the Enotocoetae, whose ears reach their feet so that they sleep in them; the Monommati, with dog's ears, one eye in the middle of the forehead, hair standing up, shaggy chests. He writes the whole catalogue out. Then he rules on it.
stops.quote: Now these statements of Megasthenes are mythical and refuted by many writers, and particularly those about the vine and wine
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 15.1.58, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 15.1.57-59, the catalogue of Indian marvels and the graded credence he gives the Brachmanes immediately after

stops.name: Amaseia, the Amazons, marvellous and beyond belief
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 11.5.1-4. Place and date of composition unknown; pin is Strabo's own city, date orders the segment.
stops.campa: The Amazons were said to have lived on the Thermodon, in his own country, and the reports about them are marvellous and beyond belief. Who could believe an army of women, or a city, or a tribe, organised without men. Strabo says so flatly and then refuses to throw the tradition out. He sets the writers against each other, checks the rivers and the mountains and the neighbouring peoples, and asks what would have to be true for it to be true. He does not settle it.
stops.quote: A peculiar thing has happened in the case of the account we have of the Amazons... they are marvellous and beyond belief. For instance, who could believe that an army of women, or a city, or a tribe, could ever be organised without men
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 11.5.3, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Strabo, Geography 11.5.1-4, the Amazon dossier as a working test of myth against evidence

stops.name: Amaseia, Typhon under the Burnt Country
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 13.4.6 (the Catacecaumene in Lydia) and 16.2.7 (the Orontes in Syria, formerly called Typhon). Place and date of composition unknown; pin is Strabo's own city, date orders the segment. The pairing of these two passages with Cilicia is a common error: neither is Cilician.
stops.campa: In Lydia there is a country they call the Burnt Land: no trees on it, ash-coloured ground, scorched rock, and vines that give a wine as good as any in the region. Some, Strabo reports, put it down to thunderbolts and to fiery outbursts from under the ground, and they do not hesitate to lay the scene of the Typhon story there. In Syria the Orontes was once called Typhon, where the dragon struck by lightning tore the channel open as it fled and forced the spring to the surface. Both accounts stand on the same page, unreconciled.
suggested_refs: The Katakekaumene volcanic field of eastern Lydia; the Orontes at Antioch

stops.name: Amaseia, Juba is lately dead
stops.date_confidence: attested at Geography 17.3.7, corroborated at 17.3.9, dating the death of Juba II of Mauretania to AD 23/24 and treating it as recent. This is the latest securely datable event in the surviving work and is the argument for a substantially Tiberian final form, against older assumptions of an Augustan edition of c.7 BC. Place of writing unknown; pin is his own city.
stops.campa: Juba, king of Mauretania, scholar, author of books on Libya and Arabia and the Assyrians, husband of Cleopatra Selene, has died, and his son Ptolemy, whose mother was the daughter of Antony and Cleopatra, has succeeded to the throne. Nothing later than this can be dated anywhere in the seventeen books. Tiberius is emperor, Augustus has been dead ten years, and a man born while Pontus was being dismantled is still at work correcting a manuscript. Strabo writes it as news: Juba died lately.
stops.quote: Now Juba died lately, but his son Ptolemy, whose mother was the daughter of Antony and Cleopatra, has succeeded to the throne.
stops.quote_source: Strabo, Geography 17.3.7, tr. H.L. Jones, Loeb Classical Library
suggested_refs: Roller, The Geography of Strabo (2014), introduction, on the Tiberian dating of the final text

stops.name: Amaseia, and then nothing further
stops.date_confidence: convention, not record. Nothing is attested about Strabo's death: no year, no place, no manner. AD 24 is arithmetic run backward from the Juba notice; retirement to Amaseia is tradition; the pin is his own city because there is nowhere else to put him. No wife, children, tomb, epitaph, ancient biography or contemporary notice survives, and no ancient portrait was ever made.
stops.campa: After that there is nothing. No ancient life of him, no epitaph, no tomb, no obituary, no wife, no children, no household, no last words, and not one writer of his own century who names him. The death date of AD 24 is arithmetic run backward from the death of Juba, and the age of eighty-seven printed alongside it is arithmetic laid on top of a birth year that is itself disputed. The bronze figure standing in Amasya today was made by people who had no likeness to work from.
suggested_refs: The modern statue of Strabo at Amasya; the Latin translation of the Geography, Rome c.1469; the Greek editio princeps, Venice 1516; Casaubon's critical edition, 1587; Aubrey Diller, The Textual Tradition of Strabo's Geography (1975)
sources: Absence of testimony across all surviving ancient sources, recorded as a gap
Roller, The Geography of Strabo (2014), introduction
